A summary and a plot describe the data you already have. To reason about data you haven't seen, you need probability... starting with what a probability even means. Say a coin lands heads with probability one half. But a single flip is heads or tails. There's no half a head. So read it the frequentist way, as the long run. A probability is the fraction of times something happens, when you repeat it over and over. That's easy to repeat in code. Flip a coin a hundred thousand times, and fifty thousand, one hundred and twenty-one come up heads. Point five zero one. Close to a half... even though the first seven flips were all heads. So how long does the long run take?

Here's the share of heads so far, after every one of five thousand flips. After four flips, it's at three quarters. Out to a hundred, it still swings from forty percent to fifty-six. After a thousand, it never strays more than a point and a half from one half. That's the law of large numbers. The short run is noisy... the long run is stable. But it doesn't work by balancing out. After five heads in a row, a fair coin is still fifty-fifty. It has no memory. A streak is never paid back. It just gets swamped by everything that comes after it. Most probabilities change, though, the moment you learn something.

Here are a thousand users, split by plan, and by whether they churned this quarter. Across everyone, a hundred and fifty churned. Fifteen percent. Now condition on the plan. Of the five hundred paid users, thirty churned... six percent. Of the five hundred free users, a hundred and twenty. Twenty-four percent. That's all conditioning is. Keep only the rows where the condition holds, and take the fraction inside them. And comparing those fractions tells you whether the two things are linked.
